summary: common.sol is the 128-line base every catalog block imports: the IERC20/IOracle/IStrategy port interfaces, the `Owned` admin mixin (inherited by 23 of 25 blocks, all but governor and timelock), `ERC20Base` (the share/stablecoin token inherited by 10 blocks: token, vault, amm, stableswap, savings, lst, safetymodule, flashlender, perps, cdp) and the `SafeTransfer` library (used by the 21 blocks that move third-party tokens). The token core is sound: the unchecked arithmetic is protected by the sum(balances)==totalSupply invariant and no block writes those slots directly, transfers revert rather than return false, and the infinite-allowance semantics are the standard Solmate ones. The worst thing found is that SafeTransfer is not actually safe: it ABI-decodes a bool from transfer/transferFrom, so every block wired to a no-return token (mainnet USDT and its forks) reverts on every pull and push, and blocks that are funded by a plain transfer in (airdrop, faucet, vesting, feesplitter) lock that funding permanently because the sweep path is push() too. Second, pull() never checks the balance delta, so fee-on-transfer or rebasing assets make the internally-accounted blocks (amm, stableswap, lending, cdp, perps, veescrow) insolvent for the last withdrawer. Third, Owned is a one-step setOwner with no zero guard, and its constructor silently makes msg.sender (a relayer, factory or the eth MCP hot wallet) the admin when 0 is passed. Nothing here lets an outsider steal funds from a correctly-configured deployment on well-behaved tokens, so the base is safe to deploy as-is with standard-returning, non-taxed, non-rebasing assets and a carefully-managed owner key; it is not safe to point at USDT or any fee/rebase token until SafeTransfer is rewritten.

findings.title: SafeTransfer requires a bool return, so USDT-class tokens revert on every pull/push and funds already inside a block are locked
findings.where: SafeTransfer.pull() L121-L123, SafeTransfer.push() L125-L127, IERC20.transfer/transferFrom L13,L16
findings.detail: Both helpers are plain typed calls through the IERC20 interface followed by `require(bool)`. Solidity 0.8 ABI-decodes the return value, so a token whose transfer/transferFrom returns no data (mainnet USDT, BNB, OMG, HT, KNC-legacy and every fork of that pattern) makes the decode step revert with empty return data, i.e. every pull() and push() against such a token reverts unconditionally. Nothing checks returndatasize, nothing tolerates an empty return, and no block wraps the call in try/catch. The failure has two faces: (a) blocks whose only entry is pull() (vault, amm, stableswap, lending, cdp, psm, staking, gauge, savings, lst, safetymodule, flashlender, perps, bonding, veescrow, strategy, treasury) can never take a deposit, which is a hard DoS of a configuration the catalog lets you build; (b) blocks that are funded by a plain ERC20 transfer INTO the contract (airdrop.sweep/claim, faucet.drip, vesting.release, feesplitter.distribute, treasury payouts) accept the tokens fine on the way in but push() reverts on the way out, so the owner's USDT is permanently stranded because the rescue path (sweep) is push() too. The helper also has no code-existence check, but that is fail-safe: a wrong or not-yet-deployed address returns empty data and reverts. This lands in all 21 blocks that declare `using SafeTransfer for IERC20`; oracle, token, governor and timelock do not move third-party tokens. (vault.sol L97 calls asset.approve() directly and would fail the same way on USDT, which also requires approve(0) first.)
findings.exploit: 1) Deploy ModMerkleAirdrop with token = 0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7 (USDT) and owner = deployer. 2) Owner calls USDT.transfer(airdrop, 1_000_000e6) to fund it (a direct transfer, does not touch SafeTransfer). 3) Any claimant calls claim(): token.push(account, amount) -> USDT.transfer returns no data -> abi decode reverts -> claim reverts. 4) Owner calls sweep(owner) after the deadline: same push(), same revert. 5) There is no other function that moves tokens out; 1,000,000 USDT is locked in the contract forever. The same sequence on ModFaucet or ModVesting strands the funded balance; on ModVault the first deposit() reverts at pull() so the block is dead on arrival.
findings.recommendation: Replace both helpers with a low-level call that tolerates an empty return: `(bool ok, bytes memory ret) = address(token).call(abi.encodeWithSelector(IERC20.transfer.selector, to, amount)); require(ok && (ret.length == 0 || abi.decode(ret, (bool))) && address(token).code.length > 0, 'PUSH_FAILED');` (this is OpenZeppelin SafeERC20.safeTransfer / Solmate SafeTransferLib). Add a matching safeApprove that sets to 0 first for vault.allocate(). Until then, the catalog should refuse or warn on the known no-return-token addresses per chain.

findings.title: pull() credits the requested amount, not the amount received: fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens make internally-accounted blocks insolvent
findings.detail: pull() returns nothing and performs no balance-delta check, so every caller does `token.pull(msg.sender, amount); state += amount;` and trusts that exactly `amount` arrived. Tokens that take a transfer fee (STA, PAXG, many taxed meme tokens, USDT if Tether ever enables its fee switch) deliver less than `amount`; rebasing tokens (stETH, AMPL, OHM-v1) change the balance out-of-band. Blocks that keep their own ledger rather than reading balanceOf(address(this)) drift from reality: ModAMM (reserve0/reserve1, amm.sol L16-L17,L66-L67), ModStableSwap (balances), ModLendingPool (per-user collateral/debt), ModCDP (collateral), ModPerpMarket (margin), ModVoteEscrow (locked), ModStaking (staked). The book says X is owed but the contract holds less than X, so the last withdrawer's push() reverts (their funds are locked) or, in AMM/StableSwap, an attacker can swap against phantom reserves. The 15 blocks that read balanceOf(address(this)) (vault, savings, lst, gauge, treasury, bonding, airdrop, faucet, vesting, feesplitter, safetymodule, staking, flashlender, strategy, psm) are accounting-consistent but still mis-credit the depositor (they receive `amount` worth of shares for less than `amount` of asset, diluting existing holders).
findings.exploit: 1) Deploy ModAMM with token0 = a 2% fee-on-transfer token FEE, token1 = USDC. 2) Alice addLiquidity(1000 FEE, 1000 USDC): pull() moves 1000 FEE from Alice, contract receives 980, reserve0 is set to 1000. 3) Bob swaps 1 wei USDC->FEE repeatedly; getAmountOut prices against reserve0=1000, so the pool sells FEE it does not have; each swap also pulls USDC that pays 2% on the way in if USDC were taxed. 4) Alice removeLiquidity(all shares): amount0 = 1000 but balance is <= 980 -> push() reverts with PUSH_FAILED (or, with a returning-false token, the same revert). Alice's USDC side is trapped because removeLiquidity is atomic across both legs. 5) Anyone who removes before Alice takes the shortfall from her.
findings.recommendation: Make pull() return the delta: `uint256 before = token.balanceOf(address(this)); ...transferFrom...; return token.balanceOf(address(this)) - before;` and have every block credit the returned value. Document that rebasing tokens are unsupported, and add a `fee-on-transfer` compatibility flag per block in catalog.json.

findings.title: Owned.setOwner is one-step with no zero-address guard; one mistyped address permanently bricks every owner gate in 23 blocks
findings.detail: setOwner() writes the new owner immediately and irrevocably. There is no pending/accept handshake, no check that the new address is non-zero, and no check that it differs from the current owner. A typo, a copy of a wrong address from the console, a contract that cannot call setOwner back, or an accidental address(0) makes the contract ownerless in one transaction, with no recovery. This is the ONLY admin primitive in the catalog: fee changes, fee recipients, strategy wiring, oracle price updates (ModFixedOracle.setPrice), airdrop root/sweep, faucet refills, timelock-less parameter changes all sit behind onlyOwner. Losing the owner on ModFixedOracle is especially bad: price() goes stale after maxStaleness and every consumer (lending, cdp, perps) starts reverting on the price read, freezing user funds behind a block that is no longer misconfigured but simply unownable. The constructor also does not emit OwnerChanged for the initial owner, so indexers cannot reconstruct ownership from events alone. Lands in all 23 Owned blocks (everything except governor and timelock).
findings.exploit: 1) Owner of ModFixedOracle (feeding ModLendingPool with maxStaleness = 1 day) intends to hand ownership to the ModTimelock at 0xAb5801a7D398351b8bE11C439e05C5B3259aeC9B but pastes 0xAb5801a7D398351b8bE11C439e05C5B3259aeC9A (last nibble wrong, no contract there). 2) setOwner() succeeds; the OwnerChanged event looks fine. 3) 24 hours later price() reverts STALE; ModLendingPool.borrow/withdraw/liquidate revert on every call. 4) Nobody can call setPrice() or setOwner() ever again; depositors' collateral is frozen until they redeploy a new oracle, which they cannot re-wire because the lending pool's oracle address is owner-set too.
findings.recommendation: Two-step transfer: `setOwner(address)` stores `pendingOwner` and emits OwnerProposed; `acceptOwner()` requires msg.sender == pendingOwner. Add `require(owner_ != address(0))` on the direct path and an explicit `renounceOwner()` that is the only way to reach address(0). Emit OwnerChanged(address(0), owner) in the constructor.

findings.title: owner_ == 0 silently falls back to msg.sender, so a relayer, factory or shared hot wallet becomes the admin and an ownerless deployment is impossible
findings.detail: The constructor turns address(0) into msg.sender instead of rejecting it. In the console path (src/app/src/app/lib/deploy.ts L44,L103) `$owner` resolves to the connected wallet, so the fallback rarely fires there. But the same bytecode is deployed from other paths: the eth MCP server's own hot wallet (the defi desk trades by calling eth/solana/bt MCP servers whose keys live there), a CREATE2 factory, a Gnosis Safe module, an account-abstraction bundler, or a script that passes 0 to mean 'nobody'. In each of those cases msg.sender is not the human and full admin rights land on a shared server key or on a contract that has no code path to call setOwner(), with no revert and no log to flag it. Conversely, a deployer who wants an immutable, ownerless instance (a fixed-supply token, a fee-less AMM) cannot express that at construction; they must deploy owned and then setOwner(0) in a second transaction, during which the owner is live. vault.sol L34 copies the same idiom for feeRecipient, so on a factory deploy performance fees are paid to the factory.
findings.exploit: 1) A user drives the defi composer through the MCP path: the plan is deployed by the eth module's server-side signer S (a hot wallet shared by every user of that box), and the owner param is 0 because the user has no browser wallet connected. 2) Every contract in the plan is constructed with owner = S (and vault.feeRecipient = S). 3) Anyone with call access to the eth module's signer (another session on the same box, an operator, a compromised API token) is now owner of the user's ModToken (can mint if mintable), ModVault (can setStrategy to a malicious strategy and allocate() the whole balance into it), ModFixedOracle (can setPrice), and so on. 4) The user sees their deployment succeed and has no on-chain signal that they do not own it: OwnerChanged is not emitted at construction.
findings.recommendation: `require(owner_ != address(0), 'NO_OWNER')` in the constructor and let callers pass msg.sender explicitly; if a fallback is really wanted, emit OwnerChanged(address(0), owner) so the choice is visible. The planner/deployer should hard-fail a plan whose $owner is unresolved rather than passing 0.

findings.title: ERC20Base accepts transfers and mints to address(0), burning value without reducing totalSupply
findings.where: _move() L93-L100, _mint() L102-L108, transfer() L78-L81, transferFrom() L83-L91
findings.detail: Neither _move nor _mint rejects to == address(0). A transfer to zero moves the balance into balanceOf[0] and emits a Transfer(from, 0, amount) that looks exactly like a burn, but totalSupply is not decremented, so totalSupply != circulating supply forever. For share tokens (vault, savings, lst, safetymodule, flashlender, perps, amm, stableswap) the shares sitting at address(0) still count in every pro-rata formula (convertToAssets = assets * shares / totalSupply), so the underlying backing those shares is stranded in the contract rather than accruing to remaining holders. _mint to zero is reachable from block code: ModVault.harvest() (vault.sol L108) mints fee shares to feeRecipient, which setFeeRecipient() (L90-L92) allows to be zero, so fee shares are minted into the void and dilute every holder for nobody's benefit. Transfer to self is safe (from -= then to += on the same slot nets to zero) and from == to on transferFrom is also safe. Lands in all 10 ERC20Base blocks.
findings.exploit: 1) Vault owner calls setFeeRecipient(address(0)) intending to 'disable' fees (there is no zero check). 2) Strategy earns 10% gain; anyone calls harvest(); convertToShares(fee) shares are minted to address(0). 3) totalSupply grew, so every depositor's convertToAssets(shares) fell by the fee fraction, and the assets that fraction represents can never be withdrawn: they are not the owner's, not the depositors', and not burnable. 4) Repeat every harvest; the vault's dead-share ratio only grows. Separately, any user who calls transfer(address(0), x) by accident loses x with a misleading burn-looking event.
findings.recommendation: `require(to != address(0), 'ZERO_TO')` in _move and _mint (OpenZeppelin ERC20 does both). Blocks that want a real burn should call _burn. Vault.setFeeRecipient should reject zero or route to owner.

findings.title: approve() has the classic allowance front-running race and there is no increase/decreaseAllowance
findings.detail: approve() overwrites the allowance unconditionally. If a holder lowers an allowance from N to M, the spender can see the pending transaction, spend N first, then spend M after it lands, for N+M total. This is inherent to ERC20 and every block that consumes share tokens through transferFrom (ModGauge staking LP shares, ModStaking on ModToken, ModVoteEscrow, ModBondDepository) inherits the race for its users. There are no increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance helpers and no permit, so the only safe pattern (approve 0, then approve M) is left to the front-end. Impact is bounded to what the holder already granted, so low.
findings.exploit: 1) Alice approves Gauge-operator contract G for 1000 vault shares. 2) Alice submits approve(G, 100) to reduce it. 3) G's operator sees it in the mempool, front-runs with transferFrom(Alice, G, 1000). 4) Alice's approve(G, 100) lands; G calls transferFrom(Alice, G, 100). 5) G took 1100 shares against an intended maximum of 1000.
findings.recommendation: Add increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance (or permit, see COMMON-9) and have the console always approve exact amounts immediately before the consuming call in the same plan step.

findings.title: IERC20.decimals() is treated as mandatory; tokens without it cannot be wired and >18-decimal tokens underflow in StableSwap
findings.where: IERC20.decimals() L17; consumers vault.sol L29, psm.sol L49-L50, stableswap.sol L55-L56,L121
findings.detail: decimals() is OPTIONAL in EIP-20, but the shared interface declares it and three blocks call it in their constructor. A token that lacks it (a handful of 2017-era tokens, some bridged wrappers, any contract that only implements the mandatory five functions) reverts the deploy of ModVault, ModPSM and ModStableSwap; that is fail-safe but the console gives the user no hint why the plan died. ModStableSwap computes 10 ** (18 - decimals): a token with more than 18 decimals (rare, but legal, e.g. YAM-v2 24) underflows and reverts, also fail-safe. ModStableSwap L121 calls coin0.decimals() at runtime in a view, so a token whose decimals() later starts reverting (upgradeable proxy) bricks that view. No funds are at risk from this finding; it is a compatibility and diagnosability issue. Blocks that inherit ERC20Base with a hard-coded 18 (everything except vault and token) are unaffected.
findings.exploit: 1) User builds vault -> strategy on a token whose contract implements only the five mandatory ERC20 functions. 2) Plan step 'deploy ModVault' reverts inside the constructor at IERC20(asset_).decimals() with empty return data. 3) The console reports a generic deploy failure; the user retries with different parameters and fails the same way until they read the bytecode.
findings.recommendation: Move decimals() out of IERC20 into an IERC20Metadata interface, and read it through a try/catch (or a staticcall that tolerates empty return) defaulting to 18. StableSwap should `require(dec <= 18)` with a clear message and cache the value rather than re-querying in a view.

findings.title: unchecked arithmetic in _move/_mint/_burn is safe under the sum(balances) == totalSupply invariant, which no block breaks
findings.detail: _move checks balanceOf[from] >= amount before the unchecked subtraction, and balanceOf[to] + amount <= totalSupply < 2**256 because every balance is bounded by totalSupply. _mint does the checked `totalSupply += amount` first, so if that does not overflow neither can the single balance it credits. _burn checks the balance and totalSupply >= balanceOf[from] by the invariant, so the unchecked totalSupply subtraction cannot underflow. The invariant holds only because balanceOf/totalSupply are written exclusively through these three functions: a grep over all 25 blocks finds no direct writes to balanceOf[...] or totalSupply (safetymodule.sol L147 only reads). Transfer to self nets to zero. This is the same pattern as Solmate ERC20 and is sound; it is recorded so that any future block that writes balanceOf directly knows it would re-open every unchecked block here.
findings.exploit: No exploit. Breaking it would require a derived contract to assign balanceOf[x] = ... or totalSupply = ... directly; none does.
findings.recommendation: Keep the invariant documented above the abstract contract and make balanceOf/totalSupply writes impossible from derived contracts (e.g. private storage with internal getters) if the catalog is opened to third-party blocks.

findings.title: Infinite-allowance short-circuit is correct; no permit (EIP-2612), no Approval event on transferFrom spend, no EIP-165
findings.detail: transferFrom skips the allowance write when allowance == type(uint256).max, which is the Uniswap/Solmate convention and means a max approval is truly unlimited (it never decays to max-amount). That is intended and gas-saving, but users who approve max to a block whose owner can later be changed (COMMON-3/4) are trusting the future owner too; nothing here is wrong, it is the semantics they should know. Since the allowance decrement emits no Approval event, off-chain allowance trackers must replay transferFrom. There is no permit(), so every block interaction is two transactions (approve, then deposit) and the plan cannot be executed gaslessly or atomically; there is no DOMAIN_SEPARATOR/nonces and no supportsInterface. Purely UX/gas.
findings.recommendation: Add EIP-2612 permit (Solmate ERC20 is a drop-in replacement for ERC20Base with identical storage layout plus nonces) so the composer can collapse approve+deposit into one signed step.

findings.title: IOracle and IStrategy carry no freshness, decimals or return values, so consumers cannot verify what they were given
findings.detail: IOracle.price() returns a single uint256 with no timestamp, round id or decimals field; the doc comment says 'scaled 1e18' but nothing enforces it. ModFixedOracle self-enforces staleness (it reverts past maxStaleness), but any other IOracle wired on the canvas (a Chainlink adapter, a TWAP block) has no standard way to signal staleness other than reverting, and a consumer has no way to distinguish 'price is 0' from 'oracle is broken'. IStrategy.deposit/withdraw return nothing and take no recipient, so ModVault must trust that withdraw(amount) moved exactly amount back and that asset() matches its own asset (vault.sol checks the latter; the former is unverifiable without a balance delta, see COMMON-2). These are interface-shape limitations rather than bugs in the shipped blocks.
findings.exploit: No direct exploit in the shipped blocks; a third-party IOracle that returns a cached price forever would be accepted by every consumer (lending, cdp, perps) without complaint.
findings.recommendation: Extend IOracle to `latest() returns (uint256 price, uint256 updatedAt)` and have consumers enforce their own max staleness; make IStrategy.withdraw return the amount actually sent and have ModVault check the balance delta.

safe_use: Do not wire mainnet USDT (or any token whose transfer/transferFrom returns no data) into any block until SafeTransfer tolerates empty return data; on Ethereum mainnet prefer USDC/DAI/WETH, on Base/Arbitrum the native USDC.
Do not use fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens (STA, PAXG, stETH, AMPL) with any block; use the wrapped non-rebasing form (wstETH) and verify the token's transfer moves exactly `amount`.
Always pass an explicit owner; never rely on the address(0) -> msg.sender fallback, and never deploy through a factory, relayer or server-side signer with owner = 0.
Treat setOwner() as irreversible: send it to a contract you have already verified can call back (a ModTimelock you control), and test the new owner on a testnet copy first; there is no undo.
Never set a fee recipient or payout address to address(0) in an ERC20Base block; the shares minted there are lost to everyone.
Approve exact amounts immediately before each deposit rather than type(uint256).max, and re-approve to 0 before lowering an allowance.
Check that the asset implements decimals() (and <= 18 for StableSwap) before adding a vault, PSM or StableSwap node to the plan.
